metric.why: A facility can have enough total cooling and still starve individual racks; airflow and pressure sensors find recirculation, bypass, and leaks that temperature averages hide.
metric.definition: Cubic feet per minute delivered through the room or containment system, and the pressure differential that drives it through equipment rather than around it.

reading.body:
Airflow and static pressure are the cooling measurements that show whether a data center's racks actually receive the cold air its total cooling capacity implies.

The metric is a pair by design. Cubic feet per minute describes how much air is delivered through the room or containment system, and the pressure differential describes whether that air is driven through equipment or around it. Its siblings in the same cooling category cover temperature and humidity at the hot and cold aisle, and liquid coolant temperature and flow rate. Read together, they treat cooling as a delivery problem rather than a capacity problem, because a facility can hold enough total cooling and still starve individual racks.

That distinction matters for compute. Temperature averages can look acceptable while recirculation, bypass, and leaks leave specific racks short of air, which means the compute in those racks is effectively unavailable regardless of how much cooling the building has installed. Airflow and pressure sensors are what expose the gap between cooling that exists and cooling that arrives.

The data does not say how any facility performs. It gives no values, no thresholds, no measurement frequency, and no instrumentation. It defines what to measure and why, not what the measurements show, and it does not distinguish AI workloads from any other compute in the building.
